| Image = [[Image:Jambalaya.JPG|300px]]
}}{{recipe}} | [[Cookbook:Meat Recipes|Meat Recipes]] | [[Cookbook:North American cuisines|North American cuisines]] | [[Cookbook:Cuisine of the United States|United States cuisine]] | [[Cookbook:Cajun cuisine|Cajun cuisine]]
__NOTOC__

'''Jambalaya''', one of [[wikipedia:Louisiana|Louisiana's]] most famous dishes, is rooted in [[wikipedia:Spanish cuisine|Spanish]] and [[wikipedia:French cuisine|French]] cuisine and is the [[wikipedia:New World|New World]] version of [[cookbook:paella recipes|paella]].

Jambalaya originated in the [[wikipedia:French Quarter|French Quarter]] of [[wikipedia:New Orleans|New Orleans]]. It was the accidental result of Spaniards attempting to make paella in the New World where [[cookbook:saffron|saffron]] was not readily available due to import costs. Consequently, tomatoes became the substitute for saffron.<ref>[http://www.crawfish.com/crawfish-jambalaya.php "Crawfish And Tasso Jambalaya."]</ref>

As time went on, French influence became strong in New Orleans, and spices from the [[wikipedia:Caribbean|Caribbean]] changed this New World paella into a unique dish. In modern Louisiana, the dish has evolved into many variations but primarily there are two types of Jambalaya: Creole and Cajun. 

Creole Jambalaya, also called red Jambalaya, is found primarily in and around New Orleans and is made with tomatoes which make it red.<ref>[http://www.elook.org/recipes/american/510.html Creole Jambalaya recipe]</ref> Cajun Jambalaya, which has no tomatoes, originated in Louisiana's rural, low-lying swamp country. It has a distinct smokey flavor and brown color, the result of browning the meat in a cast iron pot.<ref>[http://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/throwdown-with-bobby-flay/cajun-chicken-and-sausage-jambalaya-recipe/index.html Cajun Jambalaya recipe]</ref> Both versions can contain virtually any kind of meat and/or seafood but [[wikipedia:crayfish|crayfish]] (called crawfish in Louisiana) is a popular inclusion.

This famous dish is surprisingly simple to prepare and works well as an everyday meal. The below Creole Jambalaya recipe includes [[Cookbook:Meat_and_poultry#Poultry|poultry]] and [[Cookbook:Tomato|canned tomatoes]].

==Ingredients==
* 1 [[Cookbook:Bay Leaf|bay leaf]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Teaspoon|teaspoon]] [[Cookbook:Savory|savory]]
* ½ teaspoon [[Cookbook:Salt|salt]]
* 1 teaspoon dried [[Cookbook:Basil|basil]]
* 1 teaspoon [[Cookbook:Thyme|thyme]]
* 1½ teaspoons [[Cookbook:Cumin|cumin]]
* ⅓ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] [[Cookbook:Chopping|chopped]] [[Cookbook:Celery|celery]]
* ½ [[Cookbook:Tablespoon|tablespoon]] [[Cookbook:Butter|butter]]
* 14.5 [[Cookbook:Ounce|ounces]] (411 [[Cookbook:g|g]]) canned [[cookbook:tomato|tomato]]es, [[Cookbook:Dice|diced]] or torn apart
* ⅔ [[Cookbook:Cup|cup]] long-grain [[Cookbook:Rice|rice]]
* 1½ cups [[Cookbook:Chicken|chicken]] [[Cookbook:Stock|broth]]
* 2 cups cooked and chopped [[Cookbook:Turkey|turkey]] or [[Cookbook:Chicken|chicken]]
* 1 small can of sliced [[Cookbook:Mushroom|mushrooms]] (optional), drained

==Procedure==
#Mix the salt, savory, basil, thyme, and cumin together, then grind them to a powder.
#Prepare the canned tomatoes: tear them up, remove the stem ends, remove the seeds, etc. Keep the juice.
#Heat a wide pan with a lid. Lightly [[Cookbook:Frying|fry]] the celery in the butter. Soften the celery but do not brown it.
#Add everything to the pan. You can add the basil, meat, and mushrooms later if you prefer.
#Bring to a [[Cookbook:Boiling|boil]], then cover and [[Cookbook:Simmering|simmer]] for about 20 minutes. The rice will absorb the liquid.
#Discard the bay leaf.

==External Links==
*[http://www.chefpaul.com/site.php?pageID=300&view=165 Chef Paul Prudhomme's seafood jambalaya recipe]
*[http://www.foodnetwork.com/recipes/emeril-lagasse/cajun-jambalaya-recipe2/index.html Chef Emeril Lagasse's Cajun jambalaya recipe]
